title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: "She's come to stay with me," said Princess Mary. "The count and countess will be here in a few days. The countess is in a dreadful state, but Natasha herself needed to see a doctor. They insisted she come with me."
"Yes—is there a single family free of sorrow now?" said Pierre, turning to Natasha. "You know it happened on the very day we were rescued. I saw him. What a wonderful boy he was!"
Natasha looked at him, and in answer to his words her eyes widened and lit up.
"What can anyone say, what can anyone think, to console you?" said Pierre. "Nothing! Why did a boy like that, so splendid, so full of life, have to die?"
"Yes, these days it would be hard to live without faith..." Princess Mary remarked.
"Yes, yes, that's really true," Pierre broke in quickly.
"Why is it true?" Natasha asked, looking straight into Pierre's eyes.
"How can you even ask why?" said Princess Mary. "Just the thought of what's waiting for us..."
Natasha, without waiting for Princess Mary to finish, looked questioningly at Pierre again.
"And because," Pierre went on, "only someone who believes there's a God ruling us can bear a loss like hers—and... like yours."
Natasha had already opened her mouth to say something, but stopped herself. Pierre hurriedly turned away from her and went back to questioning Princess Mary about his friend's last days.

Pierre's awkwardness had almost worn off by now, but at the same time he felt that his freedom had vanished completely. He felt that there was now a judge over his every word and action, and that this judge's verdict mattered to him more than the verdict of the whole rest of the world put together. As he spoke, he found himself weighing what impression his words would make on Natasha. He wasn't saying things on purpose to please her, but whatever he said, he looked at it through her eyes.

Princess Mary—reluctantly, as people usually do in such cases—began telling him about the state she'd found Prince Andrew in. But Pierre's face, trembling with feeling, and his eager, restless questions, gradually drew her into details she had dreaded recalling even for her own sake.

"Yes, yes, and then...?" Pierre kept saying, leaning toward her with his whole body, listening eagerly to her story. "Yes, yes... so he grew calm, gentler? With his whole soul he'd always wanted just one thing—to be truly good—so he couldn't have been afraid of dying. Whatever faults he had—if he had any—weren't really his fault. So he did soften?... What a wonderful thing that he saw you again," he added, turning suddenly to Natasha and looking at her with eyes full of tears.
Natasha's face twitched. She frowned and lowered her eyes for a moment. She hesitated, unsure whether to speak.

"Yes, that was happiness," she said at last, in her quiet voice with its deep, chesty tone. "For me, it truly was happiness." She paused. "And he... he... he said he'd been wishing for it at the very moment I walked into the room...."
Natasha's voice broke. She flushed, pressed her clasped hands against her knees, then, with a visible effort at control, lifted her head and began speaking quickly.

"We knew nothing about it when we left Moscow. I didn't dare ask about him. Then suddenly Sonya told me he was traveling with us. I had no idea, I couldn't imagine what state he was in—all I wanted was to see him, to be with him," she said, trembling, breathing fast.

And without letting them interrupt, she went on to tell them what she had never told anyone before—everything she had lived through during those three weeks of the journey and of their time at Yaroslavl.

Pierre listened to her with his lips parted, his tear-filled eyes fixed on her. As he listened he wasn't thinking about Prince Andrew, or about death, or about what she was actually telling him. He listened to her and felt only pity for her—for what she was suffering right now, in the telling.
Princess Mary, frowning as she fought back her own tears, sat beside Natasha and heard, for the first time, the story of those last days of her brother's love for Natasha, and Natasha's for him.
Clearly Natasha needed to tell that story—painful as it was, and joyful too.
She talked on, mixing the most trivial details in with the innermost secrets of her heart, and it seemed as if she would never stop. Several times she repeated the same thing twice.
Dessalles' voice came from outside the door, asking whether little Nicholas could come in to say good night.
"Well, that's all of it—everything," said Natasha.

She got up quickly just as Nicholas came in, almost ran to the door hidden behind the curtains, struck her head on it, and rushed out of the room with a groan of pain or grief—it was hard to tell which.
Pierre stared at the door she had vanished through, and couldn't understand why he suddenly felt utterly alone in the world.
Princess Mary pulled him out of his daze by drawing his attention to her nephew, who had come into the room.

In that moment of tenderness, young Nicholas's face—which looked so much like his father's—moved Pierre so deeply that after kissing the boy he got up quickly, pulled out his handkerchief, and went to the window. He meant to say goodbye to Princess Mary, but she wouldn't let him go.
"No—Natasha and I sometimes don't go to sleep until after two, so please don't leave. I'll have supper brought up. Go on down, we'll join you in a moment."
Before Pierre left the room, Princess Mary told him: "This is the first time she's talked about him like that."

title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: Pierre was shown into the large, brightly lit dining room; a few minutes later he heard footsteps, and Princess Mary came in with Natasha. Natasha was calm, though a serious, grave expression had settled on her face again. All three of them now felt that awkwardness that usually follows a serious, heartfelt talk. It's impossible to go back to the same subject, talking about trifles feels awkward, and yet the urge to talk is there, so silence feels like an affectation. They went to the table without a word. The footmen pulled the chairs back and pushed them in again. Pierre unfolded his cold napkin and, determined to break the silence, looked from Natasha to Princess Mary. They had evidently both come to the same decision: both their eyes shone with the quiet satisfaction of an admission that alongside sorrow, life also holds joy.

"Will you have some vodka, Count?" asked Princess Mary, and those words suddenly banished the shadows of the past. "Now tell us about yourself," she said. "People say such unbelievable things about you."

"Yes," Pierre answered, with the smile of mild irony that had become habitual to him now. "They even tell me things I never dreamed happened to me! Mary Abramovna invited me to her house and kept telling me what had happened to me, or ought to have happened to me. Stepan Stepanych also instructed me on how I ought to tell the story of my adventures. In general I've noticed it's very easy to become an interesting man—I'm an interesting man now—people invite me over and tell me all about myself."
Natasha smiled and was about to say something.
"We were told," Princess Mary broke in, "that you lost two million rubles in Moscow. Is that true?"
"Yet I'm three times as rich as I was before," Pierre replied.
Even though his situation had actually changed now that he'd decided to pay off his wife's debts and rebuild her houses, Pierre still insisted he had become three times as rich as before.
"What I've definitely gained is freedom," he began seriously, but didn't go on, realizing the subject was too self-centered.
"And are you building?"
"Yes. Savelich says I must!"

"Tell me—did you already know about the countess's death when you decided to stay behind in Moscow?" asked Princess Mary, and immediately flushed, realizing that her question, coming right after his talk of freedom, gave his words a meaning he perhaps hadn't intended.

"No," Pierre answered, apparently not at all bothered by the meaning Princess Mary had given his words. "I heard about it in Oryol, and you can't imagine how it shook me. We weren't a model couple," he added quickly, glancing at Natasha and noticing the curiosity on her face about how he'd speak of his wife, "but her death shook me terribly. When two people quarrel, they're both always somewhat to blame, and your own guilt suddenly feels much heavier once the other person is no longer alive to answer it. And then a death like that... with no friends near her, no comfort! I feel very, very sorry for her," he finished, pleased to see a look of glad approval on Natasha's face.
"So, you're an eligible bachelor again," said Princess Mary.
Pierre suddenly flushed crimson and for a long while tried not to look at Natasha. When he finally risked a glance her way, her face seemed cold, stern—almost contemptuous, he thought.
"And is it true you actually saw and spoke with Napoleon, the way we've heard?" said Princess Mary.
Pierre laughed.
"No, not once! Everyone seems to imagine that being taken prisoner means becoming Napoleon's guest. Not only did I never see him, I never even heard anything about him—I was in far lower company!"
Supper ended, and Pierre, who at first had refused to talk about his captivity, was gradually drawn into telling the story.
"But it's true you stayed behind in Moscow to kill Napoleon?" Natasha asked with a faint smile. "I guessed as much back when we met at the Sukharev Tower—remember?"
Pierre admitted it was true, and from there, drawn on gradually by Princess Mary's questions and especially by Natasha's, he gave a detailed account of everything that had happened to him.

At first he spoke with the mild, amused irony that had become his habit toward everyone, and especially toward himself, but when he came to describing the horrors and suffering he had witnessed, he got carried away without meaning to, and began speaking with the suppressed feeling of a man reliving strong impressions in the act of recalling them.

Princess Mary, with a gentle smile, kept looking from Pierre to Natasha and back. In the whole story she saw only Pierre and his goodness. Natasha, leaning on her elbow, her expression constantly shifting with the story, watched Pierre with an attention that never wandered—clearly living through everything he described right alongside him. Not just her look, but her exclamations and the brief questions she asked, showed Pierre that she understood exactly what he was trying to convey. It was clear she grasped not only what he said, but also what he wanted to say and couldn't put into words. Pierre's account of the incident with the child and the woman—the one he'd been arrested for trying to protect—went like this: "It was an awful sight—children abandoned, some of them right in the flames... One was snatched out just in front of me... and there were women who'd had their things ripped off them, their earrings torn right out of their ears..." he flushed and grew flustered. "Then a patrol arrived and arrested every man there—every man, that is, who wasn't looting—and I was one of them."
"I'm sure you're not telling us everything—I'm sure you did something..." said Natasha, then paused and added, "something brave?"
Pierre went on. When he reached the execution he wanted to skip over the horrible details, but Natasha insisted he leave nothing out.
Pierre began to tell them about Karataev, then stopped. By now he had risen from the table and was pacing the room, Natasha following him with her eyes. Then he added:
"No—you can't understand what I learned from that man, that illiterate, simple man."
"Yes, yes, go on!" said Natasha. "Where is he now?"
"They killed him almost right in front of me."
And Pierre, his voice shaking the whole time, went on to describe the last days of the retreat, Karataev's illness, and his death.

He told the story of his adventures in a way he'd never let himself recall them before. He now saw, as it were, a new meaning in everything he had lived through. Now that he was telling it all to Natasha, he felt that particular pleasure a man feels when women listen to him—not the clever women who listen either to remember what they hear so they can use it to sharpen their own minds and repeat it later, or who want to fold it into some idea of their own and immediately offer their own clever remarks, ready-made in their little mental workshop—but the pleasure that comes from real women, gifted with the capacity to take in and absorb the very best a man has to show of himself. Natasha, without realizing it, was pure attention: she didn't miss a word, didn't miss a single quiver in Pierre's voice, not a look, not a twitch of a muscle in his face, not a single gesture. She caught his unfinished sentences in mid-flight and took them straight into her open heart, sensing the hidden meaning behind all of Pierre's inner struggle.

Princess Mary understood his story and felt for him, but by now something else had caught her full attention. She saw the possibility of love and happiness between Natasha and Pierre, and the first flicker of that thought filled her heart with gladness.
It was three in the morning. The footmen came in, their faces sad and stern, to change the candles, but no one noticed them.

Pierre finished his story. Natasha went on looking at him closely with bright, attentive, animated eyes, as though trying to make out something more that he had perhaps left unsaid. Pierre, in a happy, embarrassed confusion, glanced at her now and then, trying to think what to say next to start a new subject. Princess Mary stayed silent. None of them noticed that it was three in the morning and long past time for bed.

"People talk about misfortune and suffering," Pierre remarked, "but if right now someone asked me: 'Would you rather go back to being what you were before you were taken prisoner, or live through all of it again?'—then for heaven's sake, give me captivity and horsemeat again! We imagine that once we're thrown out of our usual ruts, everything is lost, but it's exactly then that something new and good begins. As long as there's life, there's happiness. There's so much, so much still ahead of us. I'm saying this to you," he added, turning to Natasha.
"Yes, yes," she said, answering something else entirely. "I too would wish for nothing but to live it all again from the start."
Pierre looked at her intently.
"Yes, and nothing more," said Natasha.
"That's not true, not true!" cried Pierre. "I'm not to blame for being alive and wanting to live—and neither are you."
Suddenly Natasha bowed her head, covered her face with her hands, and began to cry.
"What is it, Natasha?" said Princess Mary.
"Nothing, nothing." She smiled at Pierre through her tears. "Good night! It's time for bed."
Pierre rose and took his leave.
Princess Mary and Natasha met as usual in the bedroom. They talked about what Pierre had told them. Princess Mary didn't say what she thought of Pierre, and Natasha didn't speak of him either.
"Well, good night, Mary!" said Natasha. "You know, I'm often afraid that by not talking about him"—she meant Prince Andrew—"for fear of not doing justice to our feelings, we're forgetting him."
Princess Mary sighed deeply, which was her way of admitting Natasha had a point, but she didn't say so out loud.
"Is it possible to forget him?" she said.

"It did me so much good to tell it all today. It was hard, painful—but good, so good!" said Natasha. "I'm sure he really loved him. That's why I told him... Was it all right?" she added, suddenly blushing.
"To tell Pierre? Oh, yes. What a wonderful man he is!" said Princess Mary.

"Do you know, Mary..." Natasha suddenly said, with a mischievous smile Princess Mary hadn't seen on her face in a long time, "he's grown somehow so clean, so smooth, so fresh—as if he'd just stepped out of a Russian bathhouse; do you know what I mean? Out of a moral bathhouse. Isn't that true?"
"Yes," Princess Mary answered. "He's changed a great deal for the better."
"With a short coat and his hair cropped short; just as if—well, just as if he'd come straight from the baths... Papa used to..."
"I understand now why he"—meaning Prince Andrew—"liked no one the way he liked him," said Princess Mary.
"Yes, and yet he's completely different from him. They say men become friends precisely when they're completely different. That must be true. He really is nothing like him—in anything."
"Yes, but he's wonderful."
"Well, good night," said Natasha.
And that same mischievous smile lingered on her face for a long time afterward, as if it had simply been forgotten there.

title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: It was a long time before Pierre could fall asleep that night. He paced up and down his room, one moment turning some difficult problem over in his mind and frowning, the next suddenly shrugging his shoulders and wincing, and then smiling happily.

He was thinking about Prince Andrew, about Natasha, about their love—one moment jealous of her past, the next reproaching himself for that very feeling. It was already six in the morning, and he was still pacing the room.

"Well, what am I supposed to do if it can't be avoided? What am I to do? It's clearly meant to be," he said to himself, and undressing hastily, got into bed—happy and agitated, but without a trace of hesitation or doubt.
"Strange, impossible as this kind of happiness seems, I have to do everything in my power so that she and I become husband and wife," he told himself.
A few days earlier Pierre had decided to leave for Petersburg on Friday. When he woke up on Thursday, Savelich came in to ask about packing for the trip.

"What, to Petersburg? What's Petersburg? Who's even in Petersburg?" he asked himself, though only inwardly. "Oh, right—a long time ago, before all this happened, I did mean to go to Petersburg for some reason," he thought. "Why, though? Well, maybe I'll go anyway. What a good man he is, so attentive, remembering everything," he thought, looking at Savelich's old face, "and what a pleasant smile he has!"
"So, Savelich, you still don't want to accept your freedom?" Pierre asked him.
"What good is freedom to me, your excellency? We lived under the old count—God rest his soul!—and we've lived under you too, and never once been wronged."
"And what about your children?"
"The children will get along just the same. With masters like this, a person can live."
"But what about my heirs?" said Pierre. "Suppose I suddenly get married... it could happen," he added with an involuntary smile.
"If I may say so, your excellency, that would be a fine thing."
"How easily he takes it," thought Pierre. "He has no idea how frightening it is, how dangerous. Too soon, or too late... it's terrible!"
"So what are your orders? Are we leaving tomorrow?" asked Savelich.

"No, I'll put it off for now. I'll let you know later. Forgive me for the trouble I've caused you," said Pierre, and seeing Savelich smile, he thought: "But how odd that he doesn't know there's no Petersburg for me now, that this other matter has to be settled first! But he probably knows it perfectly well, and is only pretending not to. Should I talk it over with him, see what he thinks?" Pierre wondered. "No—another time."
At breakfast Pierre told his cousin, the princess, that he had visited Princess Mary the day before and had met there—"Guess who? Natasha Rostova!"
The princess seemed to see nothing more remarkable in that than if he'd mentioned running into Anna Semyonovna.
"Do you know her?" Pierre asked.
"I've seen the young countess," she replied. "I heard they were arranging a match for her with young Rostov. It would be a very good thing for the Rostovs—they say the family's utterly ruined."
"No—I mean, do you actually know Natasha Rostova?"
"I heard about that business of hers at the time. It was a great pity."
"No, she either doesn't understand or she's pretending," Pierre thought. "Better not say anything more to her about it."
The princess had also had provisions packed for Pierre's journey.
"How kind everyone is," thought Pierre. "What's strange is that they should still bother with these things now, when it can't possibly matter to them anymore. And all for my sake!"
That same day the Chief of Police came to see Pierre, inviting him to send someone to the Faceted Palace to collect property that was to be returned to its owners that day.

"And this man too," thought Pierre, studying the Chief of Police's face. "What a fine-looking, kind officer. Imagine troubling himself over such trifles now! And people actually say he's dishonest, that he takes bribes. What nonsense! Besides, why shouldn't he take bribes? That's how he was raised, and everyone does it. But what a kind, pleasant face, and how he smiles when he looks at me."
Pierre went to Princess Mary's for dinner.

As he drove through the streets past the burned-out houses, he found himself struck by the beauty of the ruins. The jagged chimney stacks and crumbling walls of the burned quarters of the city, stretching out and half-hiding one another, reminded him of the Rhine and of the Colosseum. The cabmen he passed and their fares, the carpenters cutting timber for new houses with their axes, the women peddlers, the shopkeepers—all of them looked at him with bright, cheerful eyes that seemed to say: "Ah, there he is! Let's see what comes of it!"

At the entrance to Princess Mary's house Pierre found himself doubting whether he had really been there the night before, whether he had really seen and talked with Natasha. "Maybe I imagined it; maybe I'll walk in and there won't be anyone there." But he had barely stepped into the room before he felt her presence with his whole being, in the loss of his sense of freedom. She was wearing the same black dress with its soft folds, her hair done the same way as the day before, and yet she was completely different. If she had looked like this when he'd walked in the day before, he could not for a single moment have failed to recognize her.

She looked the way he had known her almost as a child, and later as Prince Andrew's fiancée. A bright, questioning light shone in her eyes, and her face wore a friendly, strangely mischievous expression.
Pierre had dinner with them and would have stayed the whole evening, but Princess Mary was going to vespers, so Pierre left the house along with her.

The next day he came early, had dinner, and stayed the whole evening. Though Princess Mary and Natasha were clearly glad to see their visitor, and though all of Pierre's interest was now centered on that house, by evening they had talked their way through everything, and the conversation kept drifting from one trivial topic to another and repeatedly breaking off. He stayed so long that Princess Mary and Natasha exchanged glances, clearly wondering when he would leave. Pierre noticed this but still couldn't go. He felt uneasy and embarrassed, but he sat on because he simply could not bring himself to get up and say goodbye.
Princess Mary, seeing no end to it, was the first to rise, and complaining of a headache, began saying good night.
"So you're off to Petersburg tomorrow?" she asked.

"No, I'm not going," Pierre answered quickly, in a tone of surprise, almost offense. "Yes... no... to Petersburg? Tomorrow—but I won't say goodbye just yet. I'll come by in case you have any errands for me," he said, standing in front of Princess Mary, turning red, but making no move to leave.

Natasha gave him her hand and went out. Princess Mary, instead of leaving, sank into an armchair and looked at him with a stern, searching gaze from her deep, radiant eyes. The tiredness she had shown so plainly before had vanished completely now. With a long, deep sigh, she seemed to be settling in for a long talk.
The moment Natasha left the room, Pierre's confusion and awkwardness vanished instantly, replaced by eager excitement. He quickly pulled an armchair closer to Princess Mary.

"Yes, I wanted to tell you," he said, answering her look as though she had spoken aloud. "Princess, help me! What should I do? Can I hope? Princess, my dear friend, listen! I know everything. I know I'm not worthy of her, I know it's impossible to speak of it now. But I want to be a brother to her. No—not that. I don't want that, I can't..."
He stopped and rubbed his face and eyes with his hands.

"Well," he went on, with a visible effort to control himself and put his thoughts in order. "I don't know when I began to love her, but I have loved her, and only her, my whole life, and I love her so much that I can't imagine life without her. I can't propose to her right now, but the thought that maybe someday she could be my wife—and that I might be letting that chance slip away... that chance... it's unbearable. Tell me, can I hope? Tell me what I should do, dear princess!" he added after a pause, and touched her hand when she didn't answer.
"I've been thinking over what you told me," Princess Mary answered. "Here's what I'll say. You're right that speaking to her of love right now..."

Princess Mary stopped herself. She had been about to say that speaking of love was out of the question, but she stopped, because she had seen from the sudden change in Natasha two days earlier that far from being hurt if Pierre spoke of his love, it was exactly what she wanted.
"Speaking to her now just wouldn't do," the princess said all the same.
"But what should I do?"
"Leave it to me," said Princess Mary. "I know..."
Pierre looked straight into Princess Mary's eyes.
"Well?... Well?..." he said.
"I know that she loves—will love you," Princess Mary corrected herself.
Before she had even finished the sentence, Pierre had leapt up and seized Princess Mary's hand with a startled expression.
"What makes you say that? You think I may hope? You really think...?"
"Yes, I think so," said Princess Mary, smiling. "Write to her parents, and leave the rest to me. I'll tell her when the time is right. I want it to happen, and my heart tells me it will."
"No, it can't be! How happy I am! But it can't be.... How happy I am! No, it can't be!" Pierre kept repeating, kissing Princess Mary's hands.
"Go to Petersburg—that will be for the best. And I'll write to you," she said.
"To Petersburg? Go there? Very well, I'll go. But may I come again tomorrow?"

The next day Pierre came to say goodbye. Natasha was less animated than she'd been the day before, but that day, whenever Pierre looked at her, he sometimes felt as if he were dissolving, as if neither he nor she existed at all anymore, as if nothing existed but happiness itself. "Is it possible? No, it can't be," he told himself with every glance, every gesture, every word that filled his soul with joy.
When, saying goodbye, he took her thin, slender hand, he couldn't help holding it a little longer than he should have.

"Is it possible that this hand, this face, these eyes, all this wealth of feminine charm that still feels so strange to me, is it possible that one day it will be mine forever, as familiar to me as I am to myself?..."
"Goodbye, Count," she said aloud. "I'll look forward so much to your return," she added in a whisper.

And those simple words, her look, and the expression on her face as she said them, gave Pierre two months' worth of endless memories, interpretations, and happy daydreams. "'I'll look forward so much to your return....' Yes, yes, how exactly did she say it? Yes—'I'll look forward so much to your return.' Oh, how happy I am! What is happening to me? How happy I am!" Pierre kept saying to himself.

title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: There was nothing in Pierre's soul now anything like what had tormented him during his courtship of Helene.

He didn't repeat to himself, with that sickening flush of shame, the words he'd said, or ask, "Oh, why didn't I say that?" or "What on earth made me say 'Je vous aime'?" On the contrary, he now went back over every word he or Natasha had spoken, picturing every detail of her face, her smile, and he didn't want to change or add a single thing—only to go over it again and again. There wasn't a shadow of doubt in his mind anymore about whether what he'd set out to do was right. Only one terrible doubt sometimes crossed his mind: "Wasn't it all a dream? Could Princess Mary be mistaken? Am I not being too conceited, too sure of myself? I believe all this—and then suddenly Princess Mary tells her, and she's bound to smile and say: 'How strange! He must be fooling himself. Doesn't he know he's just a man, only a man, while I...? I'm something entirely different, something higher.'"

That was the only doubt that kept troubling Pierre. He wasn't making any plans now. The happiness in front of him seemed so unimaginable that if he could only reach it, it would be the end of everything—everything would be complete.

A joyful, unexpected kind of madness, the sort he'd never thought himself capable of, took hold of him. The whole meaning of life—not just his own life, but the whole world's—now seemed to him to be centered in his love and in the possibility of being loved by her. At times it seemed to him that everyone around him was occupied with exactly one thing: his future happiness. Sometimes it seemed to him that other people were all just as pleased as he was, and were only pretending to be busy with other things to hide it. In every word, every gesture, he saw hints of his own happiness. He often surprised the people he met with his meaningfully happy looks and smiles, which seemed to hint at some secret understanding between him and them. And when he realized that people might not actually be aware of his happiness, he felt sorry for them with his whole heart, and wanted somehow to explain to them that whatever was occupying them was a trivial, frivolous thing, not worth a moment's attention.

When people suggested he go into government service, or when the war or general political matters came up, discussed on the assumption that everyone's welfare hinged on this or that turn of events, he would listen with a mild, pitying smile, and surprise people with his strange remarks. But at this time he saw everyone—both the people who, as he imagined, understood the real meaning of life, which was to say, what he himself was feeling, and the unfortunate ones who clearly didn't understand it—all lit by the glow of the feeling shining within him, and effortlessly, without even trying, he saw in every single person he met everything good in them, everything worth loving.

When he went through his dead wife's affairs and papers, her memory stirred nothing in him but pity that she had never known the happiness he now knew. Prince Vasili, who, having landed a new post and some fresh decorations, was especially full of himself these days, struck Pierre now as a pitiable, good-natured old man, much to be felt sorry for.

Often, later in life, Pierre looked back on this period of blissful madness. Every view he formed of people and circumstances during this time stayed true for him ever afterward. Not only did he never renounce them later on, but whenever he was in doubt or torn between conflicting feelings, he would go back to the views he'd held during this time of his madness, and they always turned out to be right.

"I may have seemed strange, odd, back then," he thought, "but I wasn't as mad as I looked. Actually I was wiser then, and saw more clearly than at any other time, and understood everything worth understanding in life—because... because I was happy."

Pierre's madness consisted in this: he no longer waited, as he used to, to discover in people the particular traits he called "good qualities" before he loved them. His heart now overflowed with love on its own, and by loving people without a reason, he found undeniable reasons to love them.

title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 20
paragraphs: After Pierre left that first evening, when Natasha had said to Princess Mary with a gaily mocking smile, "He looks just—just as if he'd come out of a Russian bathhouse—in a short coat, his hair cropped short," something hidden, something Natasha herself didn't know was there, but couldn't be held back, woke up in her soul.

Everything about her—her face, her walk, her look, her voice—suddenly changed. To her own surprise, a force of life and a hope of happiness rose to the surface and demanded to be satisfied. From that evening on, she seemed to have forgotten everything that had happened to her. She no longer complained about her situation, didn't say a word about the past, and no longer feared to make happy plans for the future. She spoke little about Pierre, but whenever Princess Mary brought him up, a long-extinguished light would rekindle in her eyes, and her lips would curve into a strange smile.

The change in Natasha surprised Princess Mary at first, but once she understood what it meant, it grieved her. "Could she really have loved my brother so little that she can forget him this quickly?" she wondered, turning the change over in her mind. But whenever she was actually with Natasha, she wasn't upset with her, and she didn't reproach her. This reawakened force of life that had taken hold of Natasha was so clearly irrepressible, so clearly unexpected even to Natasha herself, that in her presence Princess Mary felt she had no right to reproach her, even inwardly.
Natasha gave herself over so fully and openly to this new feeling that she didn't even try to hide the fact that she was no longer sad, but bright and cheerful.
When Princess Mary came back to her room after her late-night talk with Pierre, Natasha met her on the threshold.
"He's spoken? Yes? He's spoken?" she kept repeating.
And a joyful yet almost pained expression, one that seemed to be asking forgiveness for her own joy, settled over Natasha's face.
"I wanted to listen at the door, but I knew you'd tell me."

Understandable and touching as the look Natasha gave her seemed to Princess Mary, and sorry as she felt for Natasha's agitation, those words stung her for a moment. She thought of her brother, and of his love.
"But what's to be done? She can't help it," the princess thought.
And with a sad, rather stern expression, she told Natasha everything Pierre had said. On hearing that he was going to Petersburg, Natasha was stunned.
"To Petersburg!" she repeated, as if she couldn't understand it.
But then, noticing the grief on Princess Mary's face, she guessed the reason for that sadness, and suddenly burst into tears.
"Mary," she said, "tell me what I should do! I'm afraid of being a bad person. Whatever you tell me, I'll do it. Just tell me...."
"Do you love him?"
"Yes," Natasha whispered.
"Then why are you crying? I'm happy for you," said Princess Mary, who, because of those tears, forgave Natasha's happiness completely.
"It won't be right away—someday. Just think how much fun it will be when I'm his wife and you marry Nicholas!"
"Natasha, I've asked you not to talk about that. Let's talk about you instead."
They sat in silence for a while.
"But why does he have to go to Petersburg?" Natasha suddenly asked, and then hurried to answer her own question. "No, no, he has to... Yes, Mary, he has to...."

title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: Seven years had passed. The storm-tossed sea of European history had settled back within its shores and seemed to have grown calm. But the mysterious forces that move humanity—mysterious because the laws governing their motion are unknown to us—went on working.

Though the surface of the sea of history looked motionless, the movement of humanity went on just as unceasingly as the flow of time itself. Various groups of people formed and dissolved; the coming formation and dissolution of kingdoms, and the displacement of whole peoples, was quietly being prepared.

The sea of history was no longer being driven spasmodically from shore to shore the way it had been before. Now it was seething in its depths. Historical figures were no longer being carried by the waves from one shore to another, as they had been. Now they seemed to spin in place. The historical figures who stood at the head of armies, and who had once reflected the movement of the masses by ordering wars, campaigns, and battles, now reflected that same restless movement through political and diplomatic maneuvering, laws, and treaties.
Historians call this activity on the part of historical figures "the reaction."

When historians deal with this period, they pass stern judgment on the historical figures they hold responsible for what they call the reaction. All the well-known people of that era—from Alexander and Napoleon down to Madame de Staël, Photius, Schelling, Fichte, Chateaubriand, and the rest—are marched before their severe tribunal and either acquitted or condemned, depending on whether they are judged to have served progress or reaction.

According to these accounts, a reaction took place in Russia too at that time, and the chief culprit, they say, was Alexander I—the very same man who, by their own account, had been the chief cause of the liberal movement at the start of his reign, and the savior of Russia besides.

There is no one left in Russian letters today, from schoolboy essayist to learned historian, who doesn't throw his own little stone at Alexander for what he did wrong during this stretch of his reign.

"He should have acted this way here, and that way there. In this instance he did well, in that instance badly. He behaved admirably at the start of his reign and during 1812, but he behaved badly by granting Poland a constitution, by forming the Holy Alliance, by handing power over to Arakcheev, by favoring Golitsyn and his mysticism, and later Shishkov and Photius. He also behaved badly by meddling in the affairs of the active army, and by disbanding the Semyonov regiment."
It would take a dozen pages to list every single reproach the historians level at him, all of it drawn from their own certainty about what is good for humanity.
What do these reproaches actually mean?

Don't the very same actions the historians praise Alexander I for—his liberal moves at the start of his reign, his struggle against Napoleon, the firmness he showed in 1812 and in the campaign of 1813—flow from the very same sources, the circumstances of his birth, his upbringing, his life, that made him the man he was, and from which the actions they blame him for—the Holy Alliance, the restoration of Poland, the reaction of 1820 and after—also flowed?
So what does the substance of these reproaches actually come down to?

It comes down to this: a historical figure like Alexander I, standing on the very highest peak of human power, with the blinding light of history trained on him; a man exposed to the strongest influences there are—the intrigue, the flattery, the self-deception that power inevitably brings with it; a man who at every single moment of his life felt himself responsible for everything happening across Europe; and a living man, not some invented character, a man who like every other man had his own personal habits, passions, impulses toward goodness, beauty, and truth—that this man, for all his undoubted virtue (even the historians don't deny him that), simply did not hold the same idea of what was good for humanity fifty years ago that a present-day professor holds, a professor who has spent his whole life since youth doing nothing but study—which is to say, reading books and lectures and taking notes on them.

But even granting that Alexander I was mistaken, fifty years ago, in his view of what was good for the people, we're forced to assume something else as well: that the historian sitting in judgment on Alexander will, after enough time has passed, turn out to have been just as mistaken in his own view of what's good for humanity. And this assumption isn't just natural, it's unavoidable—because if you watch the movement of history, you see that opinion about what's good for mankind shifts every year, with every new writer, so that what looked good ten years ago looks bad now, and the reverse. What's more, we find flatly contradictory views held at one and the same time about what counts as good and bad in history: some people count granting Poland a constitution and forming the Holy Alliance as praiseworthy acts of Alexander's, while others count the very same acts as blameworthy.

The activity of Alexander, or of Napoleon, can't rightly be called either useful or harmful, because there's no way to say what, exactly, it was useful or harmful for. If that activity displeases someone, it's only because it doesn't line up with that person's own limited idea of what's good. Whether the preservation of my father's house in Moscow, or the glory of Russian arms, or the prosperity of the universities of Petersburg and elsewhere, or the freedom of Poland, or the greatness of Russia, or the balance of power in Europe, or some particular kind of European culture called "progress," strikes me as good or bad—whichever way I judge it, I have to admit that beyond all these things, the actions of every historical figure serve other, more general purposes that I simply cannot see.

But let's grant, for argument's sake, that what we call science can reconcile all these contradictions and does possess some fixed, unchanging standard of good and bad by which to judge historical figures and events. Let's say Alexander could have done everything differently. Let's say that, guided by the very people who blame him now, people who claim to know the ultimate goal humanity is moving toward, he could have arranged everything according to the program his present-day accusers would hand him—nationality, freedom, equality, progress, let's say that about covers it. Let's assume this program was achievable, that it had already been worked out at the time, and that Alexander had acted on it. What, then, would have become of the activity of everyone who opposed the government's prevailing policy at that time—activity that the historians themselves judge to have been good and beneficial? That activity simply would not have existed. There would have been no life at all. There would have been nothing.
If we accept that human life can be governed by reason, then the very possibility of life is destroyed.

title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: If we assume, the way historians do, that great men lead humanity toward certain goals—the greatness of Russia or of France, the balance of power in Europe, the spread of the ideas of the Revolution, general progress, or anything else—then there's no way to explain the facts of history without bringing in the ideas of chance and genius.

If the goal of the European wars at the start of the nineteenth century had really been the aggrandizement of Russia, that goal could have been reached without any of the wars that came before it, and without the invasion at all. If the goal was the aggrandizement of France, that could have been reached without the Revolution and without the Empire. If the goal was spreading certain ideas, the printing press could have done that job far better than warfare ever could. If the goal was the progress of civilization, it's easy enough to see that there are other, better ways of spreading civilization than by destroying wealth and human lives.
So why did it happen this way, and not some other way?
Because that's how it happened! "Chance created the situation; genius made use of it," says history.
But what is chance? What is genius?

The words "chance" and "genius" don't point to any real, existing thing, and so they can't actually be defined. They only mark a certain stage in our understanding of events. I don't know why some particular event happens; I decide I can't know it; so I stop trying to know it, and I call it chance. I see a force producing effects that go beyond the reach of ordinary human power; I don't understand why this is happening, and I call it genius.

To a flock of rams, the one ram that the shepherd drives every evening into a separate pen to be fed, and that grows twice as fat as the rest, must look like a genius. And it must seem an astonishing coincidence of genius with a whole run of extraordinary luck that this particular ram—the one that, instead of going into the general fold every evening, goes into a special pen full of oats—that this very ram, now bursting with fat, ends up slaughtered for meat.

But all the rams would have to do is stop assuming that everything that happens to them happens purely for the sake of their own sheepish goals; they'd only have to admit that whatever happens to them might also serve purposes beyond their understanding, and right away they'd see a unity, a coherence, in everything that happened to that fattened ram. Even without knowing what purpose they were being fattened for, they would at least know that nothing that happened to the ram happened by accident, and they would no longer need the ideas of chance or genius at all.

Only by giving up our claim to make out some purpose we can immediately grasp, and by admitting that the ultimate purpose lies beyond our understanding, can we begin to see the pattern running through the experiences of historical figures and grasp the real cause behind the effects they produce, effects out of all proportion to ordinary human capacities. And once we do that, the words "chance" and "genius" become unnecessary.

We need only admit that we don't know the purpose behind the European convulsions, and that all we actually know are the facts—that is, the killing, first in France, then in Italy, in Africa, in Prussia, in Austria, in Spain, and in Russia—and that the movements from west to east and then from east to west form the essence and the point of these events. Once we admit that, we won't just have no need to see extraordinary ability and genius in Napoleon and Alexander, we'll be unable to see them as anything but men like other men, and we won't need to reach for chance to explain the small events that made these particular men what they were, because it will be plain that every one of those small events was inevitable.

By giving up any claim to know the ultimate purpose, we'll see clearly that just as no one could imagine a blossom or a seed better suited to any given plant than the ones it actually produces, so it's impossible to imagine two people more perfectly fitted, down to the smallest detail, for the purpose they had to fulfill, than Napoleon and Alexander, with everything that made them who they were.

title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: The fundamental, essential meaning of the European events of the early nineteenth century lies in the movement of the mass of European peoples from west to east, and afterward from east to west. The movement from west to east came first. For the peoples of the west to be able to make their warlike march all the way to Moscow, three things had to happen: (1) they had to form themselves into a military group of a size large enough to withstand a collision with the warlike military group of the east; (2) they had to throw off all their established traditions and customs; and (3) during their military march they had to have at their head a man who could justify to himself, and to them, the lies, the robberies, and the murders that this march would require.

And starting with the French Revolution, the old, inadequately sized group was broken apart, along with the old habits and traditions, and step by step a new group was formed, larger in scale, with new customs and new traditions, and a man was produced who could stand at the head of the coming march and carry the responsibility for everything it would take.

A man with no convictions, no habits, no traditions, not even a name of his own, not even a Frenchman, emerges—by what look like the strangest chances—from the whole seething mass of French factions, and without attaching himself to any one of them, is carried forward into a position of prominence.

The ignorance of his colleagues, the weakness and insignificance of his opponents, the sheer bluntness of his lies, and this man's dazzling, self-assured limitations, all combine to raise him to the head of the army. The brilliant qualities of the soldiers sent to Italy, his opponents' reluctance to fight, and his own childish daring and self-confidence win him military fame. Countless so-called chances follow him wherever he goes. Falling out of favor with the rulers of France turns to his advantage. His attempts to escape his predestined path all fail: he is refused a place in the Russian service, and the post he seeks in Turkey comes to nothing. During the war in Italy he comes to the brink of destruction several times, and each time is saved in some unexpected way. And thanks to various diplomatic considerations, the Russian armies—the very ones that might have destroyed his reputation—never turn up on the scene until he is already gone.

When he comes back from Italy he finds the government in Paris in the middle of falling apart—a process in which everyone attached to it is inevitably swept away and destroyed. And by chance, a way out of this dangerous position presents itself, in the form of a pointless, senseless expedition to Africa. Once again so-called chance goes with him. Impregnable Malta surrenders without a single shot fired. His most reckless schemes come off brilliantly. The enemy fleet, which afterward would not let a single boat slip past, lets his entire army through unharmed. In Africa a whole series of outrages are committed against a nearly defenseless population. And the men who commit these crimes, above all their leader, convince themselves that this is admirable, that this is glory—it resembles Caesar, it resembles Alexander the Great, and so it must be good.

This ideal of glory and grandeur—which consists not merely in seeing nothing wrong in whatever one does, but in actually taking pride in every crime one commits, treating it as if it carried some incomprehensible, almost supernatural meaning—this ideal, which would go on to guide this man and everyone around him, found room to develop in Africa. Whatever he attempts succeeds. The plague does not touch him. The cruelty of murdering prisoners is never held against him as a fault. His childish, reckless, needless, and shameful departure from Africa, abandoning his own comrades in the middle of their troubles, is chalked up to his credit, and once again the enemy fleet lets him slip past, not once but twice. And when, drunk on the crimes he has carried off so successfully, he reaches Paris, the collapse of the republican government—which a year earlier might have finished him—has now gone as far as it can go, and his arrival there, a newcomer with no ties to any faction, can only lift him higher still. And though he himself has no plan of his own, he is more than ready to step into his new role.
He had no plan, he was afraid of everything, but the factions snatched at him and demanded that he take part.

He alone—armed with his ideal of glory and grandeur, worked out in Italy and Egypt, his insane self-worship, his boldness in crime, his bluntness in lying—he alone was capable of justifying what had to be done.

He is needed to fill the place waiting for him, and so, almost against his own will, despite his indecision, his lack of any plan, and all his blunders, he is drawn into a conspiracy aimed at seizing power, and the conspiracy succeeds.

He is pushed into a meeting of the legislature. In a panic he wants to flee, believing himself finished. He pretends to fall into a swoon and babbles things that should have destroyed him. But the once proud, once shrewd rulers of France, sensing that their own part is played out, are even more confused than he is, and fail to say the words that would have destroyed him and kept their own power intact.

Chance—millions of chances—hand him power, and everyone acts as though by agreement to help secure that power for him. Chance shapes the characters of France's rulers, who submit to him. Chance shapes the character of Paul I of Russia, who recognizes his government. Chance arranges a plot against him that not only fails to hurt him but ends up confirming his power. Chance puts the Duc d'Enghien in his hands and, out of nowhere, drives him to have the man killed, thereby convincing the mob, more forcefully than anything else could, that he had the right, because he had the might. Chance sees to it that although he throws all his energy into preparing an expedition against England, one that would certainly have ruined him, he never actually carries it out, but instead unexpectedly falls upon Mack and the Austrians, who surrender without a fight. Chance and genius together hand him victory at Austerlitz; and by chance, everyone—not just the French but all of Europe, except England, which takes no part in the events about to unfold—despite their former horror and loathing of his crimes, now recognizes his authority, the title he has given himself, and his ideal of grandeur and glory, which suddenly strikes them all as excellent and reasonable.

As if sizing themselves up, as if rehearsing for the movement to come, the western forces push eastward again and again, in 1805, 1806, 1807, and 1809, gathering strength each time and growing. In 1811 the group that had formed in France merges into a single body with the peoples of Central Europe. The force of the justification behind the man at the head of this movement grows along with the size of the group. Across this ten-year period of preparation, this man has formed ties with every crowned head in Europe. The discredited rulers of the world have no reasonable ideal of their own to set against Napoleon's mad ideal of glory and grandeur. One after another they rush to parade their own insignificance before him. The King of Prussia sends his own wife to beg the great man for mercy. The Emperor of Austria counts it a favor that this man takes a daughter of the Caesars into his bed. The Pope, guardian of everything the nations hold sacred, puts religion itself to work glorifying the great man. It isn't so much Napoleon preparing himself to carry out his role, as it is everyone around him preparing him to shoulder the entire responsibility for everything that is happening and has to happen. There is no step he takes, no crime, no petty fraud, that the people around him don't instantly dress up as a great deed. The finest celebration the Germans can think up in his honor is a commemoration of Jena and Auerstädt. Not only is he great, but so are his ancestors, his brothers, his stepsons, his brothers-in-law. Everything possible is done to strip him of whatever reason he has left and to ready him for his terrible part. And by the time he is ready, so are the forces he needs.

The invasion pushes eastward and reaches its final goal, Moscow. The city is taken. The Russian army suffers heavier losses than the opposing armies suffered in the earlier fighting, from Austerlitz all the way to Wagram. But suddenly, in place of the chances and the genius that up to now had carried him, without a single break, from success to success toward his predestined goal, an endless string of chances now runs the other way, from the head cold that strikes him at Borodino to the sparks that set Moscow ablaze, to the frosts; and in place of genius, stupidity and boundless baseness come to the surface instead.
The invaders flee, turn back, flee again, and from now on all the chances run not for Napoleon but always against him.

Then a countermovement takes place from east to west, one that bears a remarkable resemblance to the movement from west to east that came before it. Attempted pushes from east to west, much like the earlier counter-movements of 1805, 1807, and 1809, come before the great westward march; there is the same coming together into a group of enormous size; the same joining of the peoples of Central Europe to the movement; the same hesitation partway through; and the same gathering speed as the goal draws near.

Paris, the final goal, is reached. The Napoleonic government and army are destroyed. Napoleon himself no longer matters at all; every one of his actions is now plainly pitiful and petty. And yet once again an inexplicable chance occurs. The allies detest Napoleon, whom they blame for their suffering. Stripped of power and authority, his crimes and his scheming laid bare, he should by rights have looked to them exactly as he had looked ten years earlier and would look again a year later: an outlaw, a brigand. But by some strange chance, no one sees him that way. His part is not finished yet. The very man who was considered an outlawed brigand ten years before, and would be considered one again a year later, is sent instead to an island two days' sail from France, an island that, for some reason, is handed over to him as his own dominion, complete with a guard of soldiers and millions of money paid to him.
